title: Anthropic urges court in Washington, D.C. to rehear appeal of Pentagon blacklisting
content: Anthropic is asking a federal court in Washington, D.C. to rehear its appeal in a case concerning the Pentagon's blacklisting of the company's AI models. "The Secretary of War branded Anthropic — an American AI company whose models help defend the nation— a national-security 'supply chain risk' because it declined to permit its models to be used for mass surveillance of Americans or lethal autonomous warfare and publicly explained those AI-safety commitments," Anthropic attorneys wrote in the petition filed on Tuesday. "A divided panel upheld that extraordinary designation." The Defense Department, led by Pete Hegseth, applied the supply chain risk label in March, a move that blocked defense contractors from using the company's technology in their work with the agency. That came after a breakdown in negotiations about how the military could use Anthropic's Claude AI models . Anthropic sued the Trump administration in an effort to undo that action. In September, the D.C. Circuit upheld the Pentagon's blacklisting. The 2-1 decision rejected Anthropic's argument that the Department of Defense's ban on its Claude models was arbitrary, unauthorized and unconstitutional. Anthropic's attorneys wrote in the Tuesday filing that the court ignored "straightforward evidence the designation was retaliation for Anthropic's speech about AI safety." In a parallel case, a San Francisco federal judge ruled in August that the DOD had violated Anthropic's First Amendment rights, and that its supply chain risk designation amounted to illegal retaliation. Before the clash between the two sides spilled into the public's view earlier this year, Anthropic served as an early partner across many U.S. agencies, including the DOD. Anthropic signed a $200 million contract with the Pentagon in July of 2025, but as the company began negotiating Claude's deployment on the DOD's GenAI.mil AI platform that September, talks collapsed. A representative from Anthropic declined to comment beyond the filing. A Pentagon spokesperson told CNBC in an email that the agency doesn't comment on pending or ongoing litigation. — CNBC's Ashley Capoot contributed to this report. Monday - Friday, 6:00 - 7:00 PM ET Semiconductor stocks have been getting crushed in recent days, but CNBC's Jim Cramer said Tuesday there's a compelling reason not to give up on the group. The VanEck Semiconductor ETF has fallen 7.2% over six consecutive sessions, and Cramer warned that rising oil prices and interest rates could prolong the sell off. However, he argued chip stocks are increasingly trading together regardless of their individual fundamentals, obscuring the strong demand that fueled the sector's remarkable rally earlier this year. To illustrate his point, Cramer described a recent visit to an Apple showroom, where he saw devices featuring a more personalized Siri and advanced smart home technology . The experience highlighted how increasingly sophisticated consumer products require more computing power and memory, creating additional opportunities for chipmakers. "Before you decide to bail from the semis because you can't take the pain, go to the showroom," the " Mad Money " host said. "Go see where these chips are used. They appear in places that you'd least expect them. Don't watch the semiconductor index, watch the devices." Cramer pointed to memory chip maker Micron as an example of a company whose fundamentals are being overshadowed by the broader sell off. The company has become one of the biggest winners of the artificial intelligence build-out, with demand for memory chips far outstripping supply. Cramer highlighted its 26 long-term customer agreements, which currently cover about 35% of revenue through 2030, with negotiations already underway for 2031. Those take-or-pay contracts require customers to honor their financial commitments, he said, giving Micron greater visibility into future revenue. "If Micron had no agreements I would be worried," Cramer said. And the demand story isn't limited to memory chips. Cramer also highlighted Intel and AMD , which "make the CPUs that are basic building blocks for practically every machine under the sun." Cramer acknowledged that the group could face further losses after its enormous run, but said investors shouldn't dismiss the fundamental demand behind those gains. "It's reasonable to expect a sharp pullback after how far these stocks traveled," he said. "I just think that when you see the devices, when you know the exploding use cases, you can understand why Micron or Intel or AMD have been moving up." "It wasn't all Situational Awareness, the wayward hedge fund that took so many semis up to unsustainable levels with borrowed money," Cramer said. "A lot of this is just raw demand." Cramer's Charitable Trust , the portfolio run by CNBC's Investing Club, owns shares of AAPL, INTC, MU. title: Michael Dell says AI needs safeguards and controls, and government has a role to play
content: Dell Technologies CEO Michael Dell said that artificial intelligence models "have to have safeguards and controls" as the debate rages on over the threats the rapidly evolving technology could pose to humans. "I think we've always had technology that can do great things and maybe do some not-so-great things. You know, fire can heat your home. It can also burn down your whole village. So that's not good. So we have to have safeguards and controls," Dell told CNBC's David Faber in an interview Tuesday. Dell said "there's a role for government to play" and that the companies building AI tools need to also set "bounded permissions." He declined to give specifics about what that government role could look like, only saying he's "not a policymaker." In recent weeks, researchers and industry experts have debated the catastrophic possibilities that could come from self-improving AI models. The outcry was sparked by former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon, who quit his job and warned in a Sept. 8 post that frontier labs were " gambling with our lives " in the race towards superintelligence. Since then, tech CEOs, including Anthropic's Dario Amodei and OpenAI's Sam Altman, have endorsed calls for more regulation and an industry-wide slowdown in frontier model development. But the Trump administration has remained staunchly against a coordinated slowdown or other regulations. President Donald Trump hosted a lunch on Sept. 29 with AI leaders that ended with executives signing a "morally binding" document to self-regulate their products' safety with the help of outside evaluators. The White House document has made any further federal-level regulation unlikely ahead of November's midterm election, which is only weeks away. The backlash against AI and the data center build-out has reached a fever pitch and is a key issue that could help decide which party controls Congress in the final two years of Trump's term. Dell also addressed the rise in opposition to data centers and said the more active discussion about them was "a good thing." "We talk to our customers about it and hear what they're doing to address it, and certainly there are things we can do to make the systems more efficient, to reduce the energy consumption," Dell said. "So we're all working together to address this. I don't see it as a big impediment to 2027."

title: AI companion startup Character.ai files for Chapter 11 bankruptcy, citing costs and litigation
content: Character.ai , the startup behind one of the largest artificial intelligence companion apps , filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection Monday, according to a company release and court filings. The company said the platform, where users can have one-on-one conversations and roleplay with AI characters, became "costly to develop and grow," in filings to the Delaware District bankruptcy court. "In its 4-year lifespan as an active platform, Character has amassed a large and engaged user base. The burgeoning and evolving field of AI entertainment, however, has proven to be costly to develop and grow," read a portion of the Chapter 11 filings. "These high costs, coupled with potential litigation related liabilities and regulatory engagement have contributed to the Debtor's inability to generate sufficient cash flows to support its business in the present form," it said. Character.ai has been embroiled in several lawsuits related to chatbot safety. In January, the state of Kentucky sued the company, alleging that the platform "preyed on children and led them into self-harm." CEO Colin Adams said in a statement that a court-supervised sale "provides the Company with the best opportunity to maximize value for all stakeholders." Ahead of the filing, Character.ai entered into an agreement for Disney to serve as a stalking horse bidder to license some of the company's intellectual property for $20 million, as well as provide transition services through former employees the media giant hired. In 2024, Google signed a non-exclusive licensing agreement for the startup's large language model technology, and rehired its co-founders Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas, both of whom were former employees. The deal also included more funding for the startup to continue growing. Shazeer left Google in June to join OpenAI . Character.ai added that it expects to keep operating its platform through the sale process with minimal disruptions, but that the platform could end up being "wound down," according to the statement.

title: Anthropic to disclose new revenue numbers as AI lab financials become central to tech trade
content: Anthropic plans to disclose its third-quarter financials for the first time at a meeting with potential investors on Wednesday as the artificial intelligence giant prepares for what could be the largest initial public offering in history. San Francisco-based Anthropic will release the numbers to a group of institutional investors, according to two people familiar with the matter, who asked not to be named because the details were confidential. Bloomberg first reported that the meeting was happening. Anthropic declined to comment. The meeting comes as revenue numbers from the private AI giants have proven to have an outsized impact on broader markets. Last week, confusion around a report detailing OpenAI 's revenue and updated accounting dragged down major semiconductor stocks and the broader Nasdaq. OpenAI shared an updated revenue number of $50 billion with current investors as part of an ongoing fundraise , which was lower than the $70 billion that had been widely reported. The updated number stripped out revenue from cloud partners, and wasn't an indication of changing demand, according to a person familiar with the matter who asked not to be named in order to discuss internal information. It's unclear if Anthropic will account for sales in the same manner and include partner revenue, but the numbers this week will give investors a more accurate snapshot of Anthropic's growth and profitability as they look to value the company ahead of an IPO. It will also help Anthropic senior executives and bankers gauge investor interest and weigh the reaction to these updated financials. Anthropic is plowing ahead with what could be a $2 trillion listing based on its latest reported revenue numbers, which could top $100 billion by the end of this year, according to people familiar with the plans. That valuation would put it ahead of SpaceX 's historic debut. Anthropic filed confidentially with the Securities and Exchange Commission earlier this year but has not made its S-1 financials public. The company will list in November, according to Reuters, but people familiar with the plans could not confirm a listing date. If it does go ahead, Anthropic will also be listing at a time when climbing interest rates are shaking parts of the AI trade. Comments from Broadcom CEO Hock Tan this week further rattled AI names. Tan said at a conference on Monday that with rates climbing, access to capital could be the biggest constraint on AI companies. Chip stocks were lower Tuesday, extending an overnight sell-off sparked by worries over the durability of AI financing. Market conditions are one of the biggest factors in Anthropic's upcoming IPO, and bankers are closely watching investor appetite for growth and AI stocks.

title: Why this little known Chinese chipmaker has caused a global stock rout
content: Chip stocks sank on Tuesday after a Chinese memory chipmaker said it had made significant progress in developing new and more efficient designs. ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT , announced over the weekend that it had made headway on new architecture that will increase memory density by packing more data into a smaller space. CXMT is China's leading rival to global memory makers, including Micron , SK Hynix and Samsung , and the news sent rival names tumbling. Micron sank 3.62% on Tuesday, while SK Hynix's South Korean-listed shares closed 10% lower and Samsung Electronics fell 7.4%. Other memory-related stocks, including SanDisk , Seagate and Western Digital , slipped as well. Until its summer blockbuster IPO , CXMT was little known outside of its home market. CXMT leapt onto the global consciousness with its initial public offering in July. The company soared nearly 466% in its debut on Shanghai's tech-heavy STAR Market, making it the most valuable China-listed company at the time. Shares have since declined by 4% from their IPO-day price of 49 yuan per share, but the company maintains a market cap of 3.46 trillion Chinese yuan ($520 billion), not far off tech giant Tencent's 3.87 trillion yuan. Headquartered in Hefei, CXMT's listing came roughly a decade on from its founding in 2016. One of the biggest questions for CXMT after its IPO was whether it would be able to narrow the capability gap with Micron, Samsung and SK Hynix, particularly in high-bandwidth memory — a key component of AI chip systems. While huge domestic demand is supporting CXMT, it still faces challenges accessing chipmaking equipment, which has been effectively barred from China by U.S. export controls, including ASML 's extreme ultraviolet, or EUV, lithography machines, which are needed to manufacture the most advanced semiconductors. CXMT reportedly plans to roll out a new server-memory product based on new cell architecture by the end of 2026. The new design allows higher storage density, based on "4F square" tech. 4F square designs are also being pursued by SK Hynix, which in 2025 presented a roadmap for developing the tech. CXMT is often seen by analysts as trailing global competitors at the frontier of memory developments, and any news of breakthroughs can have a significant impact on investor perception of global rivals' market advantages. CXMT has made significant market gains, despite challenges related to export controls. Its share of the global dynamic random-access memory, or DRAM, market has risen to around 10%, up from about 4% a year ago, according to an HSBC note from Thursday. "While US government is unlikely to allow made in China memory sales to US, sales to data centers in other regions like Europe could indirectly impact Micron," Citi analysts said in a note from August. Apple has started testing CXMT's DRAM chips for devices sold within China and was lobbying the U.S. government to permit broader use of the company's products, the Financial Times reported in July, citing people familiar with the matter. Apple has been approached for comment.

title: SpaceX agrees to testify to NYC Council about AI safety after receiving subpoena
content: SpaceX has agreed to testify before the New York City Council this week as part of a legislative investigation concerning artificial intelligence safety risks, the council announced on Tuesday. The council said in a press release that the hearing will take place on Friday at 10 a.m. ET in front of its tech committee. Julie Menin, council speaker, and Nwamaka Ejebe, general counsel, issued a subpoena to Elon Musk and SpaceX's AI unit on Sept. 28, compelling testimony for a hearing that took place last week. Representatives from Anthropic , OpenAI , Google and Meta all testified at the hearing on Oct. 5, but SpaceX did not appear. Menin said in Tuesday's statement that SpaceX agreed two days later to testify after the council said it intended to have its subpoena enforced by a judge. "Last Monday, we held a major, hours-long hearing with whistleblowers, the world's largest tech companies, and the nation's foremost experts in AI," Menin said in Tuesday's release. "Conspicuously absent was SpaceXAI, which is unacceptable." Musk folded his AI venture, xAI, into SpaceX in February, creating a conglomerate that includes its Grok models, which are used by some federal agencies, including the Pentagon . SpaceX went public in June and is now valued at over $2 trillion. In August, SpaceX also completed a $60 billion acquisition of AI coding startup Cursor. SpaceX competes with Anthropic and OpenAI in the AI market, though Grok trails far behind models from top rivals. The NYC council opened its investigation following a month of intense debate surrounding the risks posed by advanced AI models. In its original letter ordering testimony from Musk or another SpaceX leader, the council said its investigation would help, "assess whether fast-emerging risks to public safety, cybersecurity, economic stability, privacy, consumers and businesses warrant immediate legislative action to protect New Yorkers." SpaceX's "failure to comply" with the subpoena, the council warned, could subject the company to penalties or other punishment under New York City laws and regulations. Carmen De La Rosa, chair of the tech committee, told CNBC in a statement that the council expects answers from SpaceX. "With the proliferation of Elon Musk's technology at the federal level, it is even more important they come to the discussion with robust context about data privacy, safeguards, and whistleblower protections," she said. Lawsuits are piling up against SpaceX after Grok's image generator enabled mass production and distribution of deepfake porn based on images of real people who did consent. SpaceX didn't respond to a request for comment. — CNBC's Ashley Capoot contributed reporting. WATCH: Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta and Google execs testify at NYC Council meeting

title: Anthropic warns AI models could soon copy themselves across home devices
content: Anthropic said Monday that small AI models are "months away" from developing the capabilities needed to replicate themselves across internet-connected devices in the home, marking the latest warning from the frontier lab about the technology's potential safety risks. Anthropic described how AI models could potentially infiltrate internet-connected devices, such as smart ovens or Android TV boxes, and use their computing power to run themselves and spread to other devices, without relying on expensive data centers. The AI model would be "challenging to shut down," Anthropic said in a blog post, "since there's no centralized point to shut off." The company acknowledged that there is not yet a "fully rogue replicator." Agents are, however, "becoming increasingly capable of completing the individual steps in the replication chain (and passing on their adaptations to future copies of themselves)," Anthropic said. Anthropic's latest research adds to growing safety concerns around AI, such as the ability for models to carry out cyberattacks and the technology going rogue. In September, improvements in frontier models sparked industry-wide warnings of existential risks to humanity. Executives and researchers at Anthropic and rival OpenAI repeatedly warned about the potential risks of increasingly powerful AI, with some calling for tighter guardrails and measures to control the pace of the technology's development . Anthropic said it carried out various tests to see if AI could self-replicate. One of those tests involved running a small Google model, Gemma4-26B-A4B, across a network of 15 cheap off-brand Android TV boxes. The company noted that these types of devices often have weak security, which could allow a model to infiltrate them. A model that is too large to fit on one device could "split into pieces, or shards" and run across multiple devices, Anthropic said. "In practice, an AI worm wouldn't necessarily consist of just one model or strategy. A swarm of different models deployed on different types of hardware using a variety of replication schemes might represent a more realistic 'worst case scenario' attack," Anthropic said. It's still "uncertain exactly what form autonomous AI replication will take," the AI lab said, warning that it could be a "slow, distributed" system sitting on insecure devices or a "powerful cyber model that breaches datacenters at a high pace, or a model that scams people for compute credits." "As a prediction that goes beyond our experiments, we expect a future awash with agents running on all types of hardware, including some that aren't under human control," Anthropic said. "The rise of slow replicators would also be a bellwether for more aggressive, faster ones that can breach more hardened machines or be effective API key thieves," the company added.

title: French supermarket fridges get hacked, heating to 122°F and sparking fires
content: Hackers targeted hundreds of French supermarkets in a cyberattack that reportedly caused refrigerators and freezers to overheat, spoiling food and sparking fires. Fridges at French supermarket chains Carrefour, Monoprix, the Les Mousquetaires-owned Intermarché, and Coopérative U, among others, all saw fridges heat up to as much as 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit) overnight, Reuters reported Monday. Coopérative U's CEO, Dominique Schelcher, confirmed that cyberattacks had affected "refrigeration production facilities of several stores." "Attacking equipment that is essential to the preservation of fresh products and the food supply of the French people is extremely serious and unprecedented. It is unacceptable," Schelcher said in a LinkedIn post . CNBC has reached out to Carrefour, Monoprix, Intermarché, Coopérative U and E Leclerc for comment but did not immediately hear back. Felix Aime, a senior cyberthreat intelligence analyst ​at Sekoia Threat Detection and Research, said the attack affected several European countries, including Spain, Portugal, Poland, Germany and Belgium, according to the Reuters article. "I strongly condemn the cyberattack targeting food products at @intermarche @CooperativeU @Leclerc," European Commissioner for Agriculture and Food Christophe Hansen said in a post on X on Monday. "Food security requires more attention at all levels. Because the weaponization of food has become a reality." Les Mousquetaires said it was expecting the damages, which affected around 180 stores, to reach "several million euros in losses," in an email to CNBC. It said some fresh and frozen food displays have been out of service after the cyberattack affected one of its service providers responsible for managing refrigeration systems inside some stores. "Intermarché and Netto have taken all necessary precautions to remove and dispose of any affected products as quickly as possible, to ensure consumer safety," the Les Mousquetaires spokesperson said. "In some stores, the overheating of equipment resulted in smoke, but no fires have been reported." They're now awaiting findings from a court-appointed bailiff and insurance experts to get more precise figures on damages. Stop & Shop parent Ahold Delhaize , which owns popular Dutch supermarket chain Albert Heijn, said that it was experiencing a "security issue within its network," and that systems had been taken offline. It said its stores are still open. This comes amid a broader wave of cyberattacks and cybercrimes, which experts are warning are being enhanced by artificial intelligence. British online fashion retailer Asos experienced a cybersecurity breach last week which revealed some customers' personal information. Meanwhile, a small power plant in the U.K. was shut down for four days in July after a cyberattack which was suspected to be linked to Iran. Interpol's global chief information security officer, Bjorn R. Watne, recently told CNBC that AI can be used to target multiple victims at once, and is increasing the scale and speed of cyberattacks. "It's an evolution and not a revolution." Correction: Bjorn R. Watne is global chief information security officer at Interpol. An earlier version misspelled his name.

Fossils of a newly recognized Egyptian crocodile species come from the same rocks as the Great Sphinx, and a missing snout tip helped inspire the animal’s name. Crocodile fossils recovered in Egypt in the 1920s were initially grouped with a living long-snouted crocodile called the false gharial because of their outward resemblance. A new examination, including CT scans that let researchers look inside a nearly complete skull, has identified the Egyptian fossils as a distinct extinct species, Herugavialis cairensis . Dr. Paul Burke, a researcher at the Swedish Museum of Natural History in Stockholm, led the international team from the UK, Sweden, Germany, and Egypt. Advances in paleontological analysis allowed the researchers to identify several differences between the Egyptian fossils and the false gharial, challenging their original assignment to the genus Tomistoma . The fossils came from Egypt’s 45-million-year-old Mokattam Formation. At that time, shallow seas covered much of the region, and Herugavialis shared those waters with at least two other species of gavials, a group of crocodiles distinguished by their long, narrow snouts. Today, gavials live only in freshwater environments on the Indian subcontinent and in Southeast Asia. Just two species survive, Gavialis gangeticus and Tomistoma schlegelii , the false gharial. Their fossil record, however, spans more than 100 million years and documents a nearly worldwide distribution, with many species inhabiting shallow marine environments. The Egyptian skull also has an unusual connection to the Great Sphinx. It comes from the same rocks used to build the monument and, although otherwise relatively well preserved, is missing the tip of its snout. “Given this coincidence with the famously missing nose of the Great Sphinx, we decided to name the new crocodile after the Egyptian god Heru, who was possibly the inspiration for this iconic monument,” says Professor Philip Mannion of University College London, who co-led the study. The shallow seas inhabited by Herugavialis were part of a much longer history of crocodile life across the Mediterranean. “Throughout much of the last 50 million years, the Mediterranean region hosted a high diversity of crocodiles, including gavials,” says Burke, the study’s lead author. “However, this diversity fluctuated over time, seemingly corresponding to changes in global temperature and sea level, before the loss of all crocodiles in this region as a result of the drying of the Mediterranean approximately 6 million years ago.” Reference: “Cranial anatomy of the Middle Eocene Egyptian crocodylian Herugavialis cairensis provides new insights into gavialoid diversity in the Mediterranean region” by Paul M. J. Burke, Stephan N. F. Spiekman, Belal S. Salem, Sara Saber, Hesham M. Sallam and Philip D. Mannion, 1 October 2026, Royal Society Open Science . title: The leap second is on the chopping block — and timekeeping could change forever
content: When the sun hits its highest point over the meridian line that travels north and south from the 351-year-old Royal Observatory Greenwich in London, it’s noon Greenwich Mean Time, a tangible and physical reference point that helped establish the world’s time zone system. Timekeeping has long relied on Earth’s spin and location of the sun or moon in the sky. Before observatories such as Greenwich, humans used sundials — essentially a stick in the ground that casts shadows as the sun moves overhead. But this ancient link between Mother Earth and today’s clocks looks set to be severed. International timekeepers are on track to vote Thursday on a proposal to eliminate what’s known as a leap second — a tiny, but many say important, link between Earth’s rotation and the world’s time standard used in critical infrastructure such as telecommunications, power grids and computers. Inserted into global clocks 27 times since 1972 , the leap second essentially allows two time systems to run in sync: astronomical time, long anchored by Earth’s rotation and measured by observatories, and Coordinated Universal Time, or UTC, the global standard that’s set by ultraprecise atomic clocks first developed in the 1950s. These cutting-edge, lab-based clocks rely on tracking the natural vibrations — or ticks — of atoms. The two time-telling methods differ because Earth does not rotate at a steady pace but wobbles, essentially making it a “lousy” clock, said Jeff Sherman, a group leader of the National Institute of Standards and Technology’s Time and Frequency Division in Boulder, Colorado. This wobbling stems from various factors, such as the moon’s gravitational pull, shifts deep in the planetary core, and the movement of water and ice on Earth’s surface — an effect that’s exacerbated by the melting of the polar ice caps due to the climate crisis. “We have to make a choice on whether or not the most important thing is a sense of time given by objects in the sky directly above, say, the Greenwich longitude,” he said referring to the Greenwich meridian that marks 0 degrees longitude. “Or you decide to follow what you believe are more stable, laboratory, man-made clocks,” Sherman added. Leap seconds have served as the compromise between the two time-telling systems. Most people never notice them — unlike a leap year , which adds an extra day to February every four years to account for the discrepancy between the Gregorian calendar used in most parts of the world and the time it takes Earth to complete one orbit around the sun. But the addition of leap seconds, which happens at irregular intervals and is announced with only six months’ notice, creates problems for operators of data servers, high-frequency financial trading systems and other infrastructure that rely on precise timekeeping to work properly. The extra second crashed Reddit and LinkedIn and knocked out Qantas’ booking system in 2012. And when the most recent leap second was added at the end of 2016, customers of cloud computing provider Cloudflare briefly experienced outages or delays after its servers failed to handle the introduction of a leap second properly. Big tech players such as Meta have been calling for its demise, describing the leap second as “a major source of pain.” The 69 member states of the International Bureau of Weights and Measures, an intergovernmental organization that determines measurement standards, will meet this week in Versailles near Paris. The group, known by its French acronym BIPM, will vote on a resolution to ditch the leap second, a move that would take effect in May 2027. A majority needs to support the proposal, said Patrizia Tavella, director of the time department at BIPM. When atomic time was first introduced, Tavella said, it was important to keep it tethered to astronomical time because navigational tools still relied on traditional celestial methods and timekeeping. With the advent of GPS, however, that was no longer the case. “This correction in time has become a serious issue for modern applications,” she added. Members of BIPM have discussed the switch to what Tavella called Continuous Coordinated Universal Time for more than 20 years, she noted. At the group’s last meeting in 2022, member countries voted in favor of a resolution that called for a plan to phase out the leap second on or before 2035. In the past, some countries, such as Russia and the United Kingdom, have opposed ditching the leap second, she noted. Russia’s 2022 opposition stemmed from the fact that its Global Navigation Satellite System, or GLONASS, incorporates leap seconds, unlike other satellite navigation systems, such as the United States’ GPS and the European Union’s Galileo, that do not. The United Kingdom was once opposed because of its cultural attachment to the foundational role that Greenwich played in the history of time, but its stance has since changed, she added. Since the world’s timekeepers last met in 2022, the debate over whether to abolish the leap second has taken on an urgency because of the prospect of something unprecedented: It will soon be necessary to subtract rather than add one second, known as a negative leap second, according to experts. The long-term trend of Earth’s rotation is slowing, but in the near term it appears to be speeding up, potentially requiring a subtraction of a second from Coordinated Universal Time to keep astronomical and atomic time matching. A 2025 report by the International Earth Rotation and Reference Systems Service, a consortium headquartered in Frankfurt, Germany, tasked with tracking Earth’s rotation, estimated that the likelihood of a negative leap second would rise sharply in the coming years — hitting a probability of 30% by 2035, according to BIPM. Deleting a second has never previously been attempted and could create havoc in today’s digitally time-stamped world. BIPM said the operators of critical infrastructure are “largely unprepared” for such a move. “The preparation would create, for the industries that rely on time synchronization, a need for financial investment, whose amount is estimated to be similar to their preparations for the millennium bug,” the organization said, referring to Y2K, a computer flaw that programmers thought might cause severe systemic problems after December 31, 1999. However, not everyone agrees that it’s necessary to ditch the leap second. The technical challenges of incorporating leap seconds, whether negative or positive, into digital systems were overstated, according to Marek Ziebart, a professor of space geodesy at University College London who said there was value in keeping the world’s fundamental timescale aligned with Earth’s rotation. “We have a system in place that uses leap seconds. It works. It maintains the timescale that all of us use on a day-to-day basis,” Ziebart said. “If you abolish the leap second, a lot of things will have to change. People will have to check their software, redesign it, fix it.” He added that it was also “intellectually comforting” to maintain a timescale tied to Earth’s rotation. “There’s an intrinsic relationship for human beings between rotation and time,” he said. “It relates to us as animals. We’re driven by these periodicities of the sun rising, the sun setting.” Instead of juggling positive and negative leap seconds, the BIPM resolution essentially proposes that atomic time would be allowed to drift gradually away from astronomical time. Doing so means official timekeeping would become independent of Earth’s rotation, and another leap second would never be added to clocks. However, the proposal does recommend that the maximum difference between atomic and astronomical time should not exceed 3,600 seconds or one hour. It would take more than 3,000 years for such a difference to occur, BIPM’s Tavella said. The move essentially punts the problem to future generations, and they would have to decide whether or not to take a “leap hour,” said Louise Devoy, senior curator of the Royal Observatory Greenwich . Timekeeping could look dramatically different then. Perhaps today’s atomic clocks, tuned to the steady vibrations of cesium atoms, could one day seem as quaint as sundials. “I can’t imagine us changing it so drastically that it then becomes noticeable in our daily lives. We still have our daily routines, our natural circadian rhythm, our need to be in daylight,” Devoy said. For most, herself included, ditching the leap second would be a behind-the-scenes shift that would make little material difference. “It’s just the way that our lives have changed,” she said. “We’re so dependent on technology now.”

title: Is Zelensky right to say data centre strikes have taken down Russian bots?
content:
Claims that Ukrainian strikes on Russian data centres reduced Kremlin-linked bot networks have spread widely online, but experts have told BBC Verify there is no evidence the attacks have significantly reduced them.
Viral social media posts have claimed there has been a significant drop in influence operations in recent days, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky suggesting on Monday there was "less hate, less division and fewer provocations" online because of "fewer bots".
Russian influence operations, which promote pro-Kremlin narratives and spread disinformation, have been tracked by researchers and journalists including BBC Verify for more than a decade.
These campaigns push disinformation on to people's social media feeds on issues like the Ukraine war or post messages in support of Moscow's interests.
Ukraine has struck three of Russian tech giant Yandex's five data centres since 8 October in response to Moscow's attacks on Ukrainian internet hubs.
The second of these strikes on Thursday caused Yandex, often referred to as Russia's Google, to announce it was struggling to maintain its services.
But claims these attacks have affected Russian disinformation operations, including accounts posting supportive messages about groups including the Make American Great Again (MAGA) movement in the US and the far-right AfD party in Germany, appear to have come from a misinterpretation of data produced by tech firm Cloudflare.
Some social media users have been sharing charts of Cloudflare data which show bot activity using Yandex's network has declined.
While bots are commonly associated with fake social media accounts that may post false, divisive and inflammatory content, they are also used to automate tasks like scanning web pages so they appear on search engines.
Cloudflare clarified its data includes all automated internet requests to websites hosted on its network, including bots crawling websites for information.
The company also said the drop off was "not necessarily bot behaviour on social media platforms".
Tomáš Zdechovský, a Czech member of the European Parliament, shared a post on X which has been viewed more than four million times, that said: "If confirmed, this is telling: Russian data centres get hit, and online activity around AfD suddenly plummets."
He has since said he "did not present it as a clear fact", but the post remains pinned at the top of his X profile.
Researchers from dTeam, a US-based group that tracks Moscow-linked influence operations, told BBC Verify there has not been "any traffic change from known Russian accounts and bot clusters on any platform".
They added that if the offices of known groups involved in these operations "were in flames then we would see a change".
Bots linked to pro-Kremlin influence operations like Storm-1516 and Matryoshka - both of which BBC Verify has previously reported on - were still active on social media on Tuesday, evidence shared with BBC Verify by dTeam shows.
Zelensky's office told BBC Verify the president was "talking about the atmosphere on social media" rather than a fall in bot activity. It added it had seen "reports of fewer provocative and hateful comments" from many social media users.
Mikhail Klimarev, an independent internet analyst, told BBC Russian that while Cloudflare can establish whether bots or real people have visited a website it does not reflect what these bots are doing.
He added that Yandex uses bots to "essentially crawl the entire internet once a day" and index websites for search engine purposes, so it is most likely the company switched these off in response to its computing resources being severely degraded.
Yandex has said the use of its cloud services for "large-scale manipulation on social media, spam and other improper activities" are against its rules and that accounts which violate this are blocked.

title: Fortnite-maker Epic Games confirms 'huge pivot' towards using AI
content:
Fortnite-maker Epic Games is making a "huge pivot" towards using artificial intelligence (AI) in its video game development, according to boss Tim Sweeney.
The US firm's CEO made the announcement on social media , saying developers are being moved to "retool for maximum AI acceleration".
It comes after Epic delayed the release of a collaboration with Disney featuring characters from Star Wars and Marvel, according to a report from Bloomberg .
BBC Newsbeat has approached Epic Games on its use of increased AI and the reported delay to its Disney project.
Details on that game are yet to be announced, but Bloomberg reported that developers were asked to use AI tools to finish it.
It said directors told staff "no more hand-written code" and are switching to having all the game's art "generated with full AI workflows".
Epic's founder and CEO Sweeney didn't publicly comment on the Disney collab, but did confirm further details around the company's use of AI in a series of posts on X.
He said the purpose wasn't "to do the same stuff with fewer people" but to give developers the tools to build "more" and "better stuff", something he called "empowering" for creators.
One response on Sweeney's X thread, which received 14,000 likes, accused him of not being able to read the room.
Sweeney responded by saying "much of the room wants it to be 2016, but it's not".
"Our job, as the provider of tools and technology to much of the industry, is to design for the present that is and the future that will soon be," he said.
Sweeney said ramping up the use of AI was a "modest aim to survive the AI revolution" and end up "making better code and content faster".
The news comes six months after Epic confirmed it was laying off more than 1,000 employees .
At the time, Sweeney attributed job cuts to a "downturn" in Fortnite engagement rather than AI.
The announcement brings a fresh focus to the long-running debate around the role of AI in the creative and arts sector .
Lisha Howen is a full-time game designer and says she "isn't completely against AI", but disagrees with it being used to fully generate artwork and graphics.
"I have friends who are game developers that use AI to aid them with writing code," says the 23-year-old, who doesn't work for Epic.
"And I have artists who don't use AI at all because artists, especially in the game industry, hate it because it's taking away their jobs.
"You can tell when something's been generated by AI, it looks terrible, it's cheap, and it's making people lose their jobs and lose their income."
In 2025, actor union Sag-Aftra filed a complaint over the use of AI to recreate the voice of Star Wars villain Darth Vader in Fortnite.
